questions.q: What does HS256 stand for in a JWT alg header?
o: High-Security 256-bit encryption of the JWT payload body
HMAC with SHA-256 using one shared secret for both operations
Hash-Salt 256, a password hashing scheme used in JWT headers
Hybrid Signing 256-bit mode mixing RSA and HMAC in one token
questions.x: HS256 is HMAC-SHA256. One shared secret both creates and verifies the signature. Anyone who knows that secret can forge valid tokens.
questions.h: HS and 256 are two abbreviations. What common MAC algorithm does HS stand for, and what hash size is 256?

questions.q: Why can a weak HS256 JWT secret be cracked fully offline?
o: The server caches HMAC results so guesses never need a new request
The token already holds header, payload, and signature for local tests
JWT servers expose a dedicated key-recovery debugging endpoint
The HMAC secret is published in the JWKS document for all clients
questions.x: HMAC verification only needs the algorithm, the header.payload bytes, and a candidate key. All of that is in the captured JWT, so wordlist tests run locally at GPU speed.
questions.h: What inputs does HMAC verification need? Are all of them already present in a captured JWT?

questions.q: Which hashcat mode is used to crack JWT HS256 secrets?
o: Mode 1000, the NTLM hash mode used for Windows passwords
Mode 16500, the dedicated hashcat mode for JWT HMAC secrets
Mode 3200, the bcrypt mode used for slow password hashes
Mode 18300, the Apple Keychain mode for macOS credential dumps
questions.x: Hashcat mode 16500 is built for JWTs. It takes the full token, tries each wordlist entry as the HMAC secret, and reports a hit when the computed signature matches.
questions.h: Hashcat has a dedicated JWT mode whose number sits in the 16000 range.

questions.q: Which wordlist is typically used to crack JWT secrets in this attack class?
o: rockyou.txt, because it lists leaked end-user account passwords
jwt.secrets.list from SecLists, covering common copied JWT secrets
A random hex dictionary covering every possible 32-byte key
The target application's compiled binary extracted from the host
questions.x: jwt.secrets.list is a curated list of secrets copied from tutorials, docs examples, and leaked configs. Developers often paste those strings unchanged.
questions.h: General password lists work, but SecLists has a purpose-built list specifically for JWT signing secrets.

questions.q: Once the HS256 secret is cracked, how do you forge an admin token?
o: Submit the cracked secret to the server authenticate endpoint
Change sub to administrator and re-sign the token with HS256
The cracked secret unlocks a hidden admin route with no token
Decode the token, drop the signature, and add an admin header
questions.x: With the secret you can HMAC any payload you choose. Change sub to administrator, sign header.payload with HS256 and the cracked secret, and the server accepts it.
questions.h: Knowing the secret means you can produce a valid signature. What payload change is still required for admin access?

questions.q: What entropy is recommended for a production HS256 JWT secret?
o: Eight printable characters, similar to a typical user password
At least 256 bits of cryptographically random secret material
Any human-chosen string that is longer than twenty characters
A UUID, which provides 128 bits and is unique per deployment
questions.x: The secret should have at least as much entropy as the hash output, 256 bits for SHA-256. A 32-byte CSPRNG value meets that. Human-readable strings almost never do.
questions.h: The 256 in HS256 is a hint. How many bits of entropy should the secret have to match the hash?

questions.q: Why is a JWT secret copied from a tutorial or README dangerous?
o: Tutorial keys expire after a published date in the README file
The same string appears in public wordlists and cracks quickly
Tutorial secrets force a weak algorithm that cannot be changed
They are encrypted with a public key that anyone can download
questions.x: Strings such as your-secret-key, supersecret, or jwt_secret appear in JWT-focused wordlists because developers paste them from docs without changing them.
questions.h: If thousands of developers copy the same docs string, is that value still a secret?

questions.q: Which of the following is true of this lab's HS256 cracking attack?
o: HS256 is asymmetric, so a wordlist cannot recover the signing key
hashcat mode 1000 is the dedicated mode used for JWT HMAC secrets
None of these statements are true about this weak HS256 JWT lab
After cracking, you only change alg to none and skip re-signing
questions.x: HS256 is symmetric, so wordlists can recover a weak secret. JWT cracking uses hashcat mode 16500, not 1000. You must re-sign with the cracked secret after changing sub.
questions.h: Check each claim against HS256 being symmetric, the JWT hashcat mode number, and whether re-signing is required.

questions.q: After cracking the secret, which payload claim is changed to reach /admin?
o: alg
iat
sub
kid
questions.x: The sub (subject) claim holds the authenticated username. Changing it to administrator and re-signing with the cracked secret produces a token the server treats as admin.
questions.h: You need to impersonate a different user. Which JWT claim identifies who is authenticated?

questions.q: What is the primary advantage of switching from HS256 to RS256?
o: RS256 tokens are shorter on the wire than HS256 and cheaper to send
The private signing key never leaves the server, unlike a shared HMAC secret
RS256 skips cryptography entirely, leaving nothing for an attacker to crack
RS256 is immune to algorithm confusion even if alg is attacker-controlled
questions.x: RS256 uses an asymmetric pair. The private key signs and stays on the server. The public key only verifies. A leaked public key cannot forge tokens without the private key.
questions.h: Compare symmetric HMAC to asymmetric RSA. Who can create a signature versus who can only verify one?
